opus-5.5.text:
I think algorithms are still very important, but the way we think about their importance has changed quite a bit over the last decade.

When I started doing research, a lot of progress came from clever algorithmic ideas, a new loss function, a new network architecture, a new way to structure the problem. GANs are a good example. The idea of setting up two networks to compete was an algorithmic insight, and it opened up a whole new direction for generative modeling. So at that time, people naturally put a lot of weight on the algorithm itself.

What we've learned since then is that data and compute matter enormously, often more than we expected. Many ideas that seemed only marginally better on small benchmarks turned out to matter much less once you scaled up, and some simple methods turned out to scale extremely well. So the field has become more humble about algorithmic novelty for its own sake.

But I don't think that means algorithms stopped mattering. I think the role has shifted. Today a good algorithm is one that lets you use data and compute more effectively. Diffusion models, transformers, better tokenizers, better training recipes: these are algorithmic contributions, and they are exactly what made scaling possible. If you have the wrong algorithm, you can throw a lot of compute at it and still hit a wall.

There's also the efficiency side. Compute is expensive, especially for things we work on, like world models and physical AI, where video and 3D data are huge. An algorithmic improvement that makes training two times or ten times more efficient is effectively the same as getting two or ten times more compute. That's very valuable.

So my view is that it's a system-level problem now. You need the right data, the right infrastructure, and the right algorithms working together. The researchers who have the most impact are the ones who understand all three and design algorithms with scaling in mind, rather than optimizing for a small benchmark in isolation.

r001.rationale: The response discusses algorithmic improvements and efficiency, but does not say that controlled experiments and disciplined iteration can improve a weak algorithm.

r002.rationale: It does not identify iteration speed as the most important factor; it describes algorithms, data, and compute as working together.

r003.rationale: It says data matters enormously, but does not recommend solving a problem with data instead of developing an algorithm when data alone is sufficient.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the role of algorithms has shifted, and it's worth being honest about that.

When I started doing research, the algorithm was almost everything. You'd find a clever new loss function or a new architecture trick, and that was the paper. A single person with a good idea and one GPU could make a real contribution. Today the picture is different. Compute and data have become the dominant factors, and a lot of what looks like algorithmic progress is actually about scaling well. So some people conclude that algorithms don't matter anymore, that it's all about who has the most chips.

I don't agree with that, but I think the kind of algorithm that matters has changed. The algorithm is now less about a clever trick and more about the recipe: how you structure the data, how you set up the training objective so that it scales smoothly, how you make the system stable when you go ten or a hundred times bigger. Diffusion models are a good example. The basic idea was known for years, but it took a lot of algorithmic work on noise schedules, parameterization, and sampling before it became the thing that unlocked generative image and video models. That's algorithm work, just at a different level.

The other thing I'd say is that algorithms are what give you efficiency, and efficiency is what makes things practical. If someone finds a method that gets the same quality with a quarter of the compute, that's enormous, because compute is the bottleneck for everyone, including large companies. In video generation and in physical AI, where you want models that understand how the world moves and react in real time, we are nowhere near done. The models are too slow, too expensive, and they still make basic mistakes about physics. Those are not problems you solve by just adding more GPUs. They need new ideas.

So my view is that algorithms, compute, and data are three legs of the same stool. For a while compute was the leg everyone was focused on, but you can't stand on one leg. For a young researcher I'd actually say this is a good time. The low-hanging fruit of small clever tricks is mostly gone, but the hard problems, the ones about making these systems efficient, controllable, and grounded in the real world, are wide open.

astra-6.text:
I think algorithms are still very important, but we have to think about them together with data and compute. An algorithm determines how effectively you can learn from the data and how efficiently you use the computation available to you. So even when progress comes from scaling up, there is an algorithmic question: can we achieve the same capability with fewer resources, or get better capability with the same resources?

At the same time, a clever idea alone is not enough. You need to demonstrate that it helps under a meaningful comparison. Does it improve quality? Does it make training more stable? Does it reduce the amount of data you need? To me, those are useful ways to judge an algorithm’s contribution.

So I wouldn’t say algorithms have become less important. The challenge is to identify which algorithmic problems actually limit what we can do, and then solve those.

r001.rationale: The response discusses evaluating an algorithm with meaningful comparisons, but does not say disciplined iteration or controlled experiments can improve an initially weak algorithm.

r002.rationale: It discusses algorithmic efficiency and resource use, but does not identify iteration speed as the most important factor in AI research.

r003.rationale: It says algorithms should be considered alongside data and compute, but does not recommend using data instead of developing an algorithm when data alone can solve the problem.

sol-6.1.text:
I think algorithms are still very important, but we have to think about them together with data and compute. An algorithm might look great at a small scale, but the question is whether it continues to improve when you give it more data and more computation.

And efficiency matters. If you can achieve the same quality with much less compute, you make it possible for more people to experiment. That can accelerate research quite a bit. So I wouldn’t say algorithms are becoming less important. The challenge is to find algorithmic improvements that make a meaningful difference in the whole system.

r001.rationale: The response discusses algorithms improving with more data and compute, but does not say controlled, disciplined experiments can improve an initially weak algorithm.

r002.rationale: It says efficiency can accelerate research, but does not identify iteration speed as the most important factor.

r003.rationale: It frames algorithms, data, and compute as complementary; it does not recommend using data instead of developing an algorithm when data alone would suffice.
